newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-US moves to spur WTO fin services talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-US moves to spur WTO fin services talks.

text.p: The United States moved on Monday to spur World Trade Organisation (WTO) talks on a global pact to open up financial services by holding out the prospect of equal access to its market for all other countries in the body.

But a new U.S. offer tabled as a fresh round got under way in the negotiations, facing a mid-December deadline, was coupled with a warning that key emerging economies would have to pledge deep-going liberalisation to make a deal possible.

And a U.S. official in Geneva told reporters Washington was "very disappointed" that a Japanese offer tabled last Friday did not reflect bilateral accords between the two countries in opening up the insurance sector.

A statement in Washington hours after the offer was delivered to the WTO said it would provide "substantially full market access and national treatment to foreign banking, securities and insurance service suppliers."
Signed by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, it repeated earlier U.S. calls for similar moves by the major developing countries.

"To make this offer permanent....it is critical that our trading partners, especially the key emerging markets, submit significantly improved offers that establish a level playing field for U.S. firms to compete effectively," they declared.

The U.S. official in Geneva said the package "fully incorporates financial sector liberalisation undertaken in our market," the world's largest, and included "important improvements" to the Washington offer presently on the table.

Delivery of the package to the WTO followed new offers by Japan last Friday and by the European Union two weeks ago. Canada, the fourth top trade power, was expected to table its latest package by Wednesday.

"First and foremost, the United States is proposing to lock in a broad Most Favoured Nation (MFN) commitment to provide access to the world's largest and most open financial market," a separate U.S. statement in Geneva on the package said.
Washington pulled out of the last bid to reach a pact in 1995. It argued that proposals from key emerging economies were not enough to justify it offering full MFN.
Under MFN, a basic principle of the WTO, countries commit themselves not to discriminate among trading partners by imposing varying terms on access to its markets.
Speaking to reporters on condition of anonymity, the U.S. official in Geneva said Washington was disappointed many other countries in the talks had not tabled new offers by Monday.
All WTO members had agreed in principle last month to have fresh packages ready for this week's round of multilateral and bilateral discussions in Geneva.
"We look to them now to put their offers on the table so we can begin intensive negotiations," the official said. Hard talking in the drive for a deal is not expected before autumn.
When the 1995 talks were on the verge of collapse with the U.S. walkout, the EU convinced other countries to agree to an interim deal excluding the United States.
But that accord expires at year end and there is no support for its continuation. Participants say a long-term pact is of little value if it does not cover the U.S. market.
The U.S. official said Washington wanted better offers from major Asian and Latin American countries but also wanted improvements from African nations and ex-communist states in Europe.

Senior trade negotiator Jeffrey Lang and a top official from the U.S. Treasury Department will tour several Asian capitals, including Seoul, Manila, Jakarta and New Delhi, in August "in an effort to push Asian countries forward," the official added.
